title: Given an array of integers, find the leftmost pivot index where the sum of all elements strictly to its left equals the sum of all elements strictly to its right, returning minus one if no such index exists. Solve it with the prefix-sum pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Find Pivot Index (Balance Point of an Array)

s1_definition.profdef: The pivot index problem asks for the leftmost index at which the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it, where the element at the index itself belongs to neither side. It is solved in linear time by first computing the total sum, then scanning left to right maintaining a running left sum: at each index the right sum is the total minus the left sum minus the current element, and the index is a pivot when the left sum equals that right sum.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh lays out a row of daily settlement amounts and wants the single day that acts as a perfect balance point, where everything settled before that day totals exactly what settled after it, with that day's own amount sitting on the fulcrum belonging to neither side. He adds up the whole row once, then walks across keeping a running total of what is behind him, and checks at each day whether behind equals ahead.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each index, left sum equals total minus left sum minus the current element marks a pivot.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The pivot index problem asks for the leftmost index at which the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it, where the element at the index itself belongs to neither side. It is solved in linear time by first computing the total sum, then scanning left to right maintaining a running left sum: at each index the right sum is the total minus the left sum minus the current element, and the index is a pivot when the left sum equals that right sum.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh lays out a row of daily settlement amounts and wants the single day that acts as a perfect balance point, where everything settled before that day totals exactly what settled after it, with that day's own amount sitting on the fulcrum belonging to neither side. He adds up the whole row once, then walks across keeping a running total of what is behind him, and checks at each day whether behind equals ahead.

**One line to remember:** At each index, left sum equals total minus left sum minus the current element marks a pivot.

sections.s2_technical:
This is a direct application of prefix sums, but it only needs a single running prefix rather than a stored map. We first compute the total sum of the array in one pass. Then we scan from left to right maintaining a running left sum, which is the sum of all elements strictly before the current index. Before adding the current element to the left sum, the sum of all elements strictly after the current index is the total minus the left sum minus the current element.

The condition for the current index to be a pivot is that the left sum equals the right sum, which we can write without computing the right sum separately as `leftSum == total - leftSum - nums[i]`. If this holds we return the current index immediately, because we want the leftmost pivot. If it does not hold we add the current element to the left sum with `leftSum += nums[i]` and continue. For example the loop body is `if (leftSum == total - leftSum - nums[i]) return i; leftSum += nums[i];`.

Several edge cases deserve attention. The first index can be a pivot if the sum of everything after it is zero, because the left side is empty and counts as zero. Likewise the last index can be a pivot if everything before it sums to zero. Negative numbers are fully supported because we are comparing sums, not using any window monotonicity. The senior-level nuance is that the current element must be excluded from both sides, which is exactly why the condition subtracts the current element once from the total when forming the right sum.

Because we return the first index that satisfies the condition, we get the leftmost pivot naturally, and we return minus one if the loop finishes without finding one. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass for the total and one pass for the scan, and the space complexity is O(1), just a couple of running totals. This single-running-prefix technique is the clean standard solution for balance-point problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the settlement operations team lays out a day's sequence of net settlement amounts and wants to find a balance-point transaction, the earliest transaction such that the total of all settlements before it exactly equals the total of all settlements after it, with that transaction itself excluded. This balance point is used to split the day's settlement batch into two halves of equal net value for parallel downstream processing. This is exactly the pivot index problem.

Problem 2 — Recomputing the left and right sums from scratch at every candidate index is quadratic and too slow for the large settlement batches the bank processes. Precomputing the total once and maintaining a single running left sum finds the balance point in a single linear scan, which keeps the batch-splitting step fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `SettlementBalancer` service with a `findBalancePoint` method implementing the prefix-sum scan, and a runnable `PivotIndexDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's settlement sequences, logging each checked index at fine level and the balance point at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's settlements are 1, 7, 3, 6, 5, 6. First we compute the total in one pass, which is 1 plus 7 plus 3 plus 6 plus 5 plus 6 equals 28. Then we scan with a left sum starting at 0.

Step 1 at index 0, value 1: right sum is 28 minus 0 minus 1 equals 27. Left 0 is not 27, so we add 1 to the left sum, left sum becomes 1.

Step 2 at index 1, value 7: right sum is 28 minus 1 minus 7 equals 20. Left 1 is not 20, left sum becomes 8.

Step 3 at index 2, value 3: right sum is 28 minus 8 minus 3 equals 17. Left 8 is not 17, left sum becomes 11.

Step 4 at index 3, value 6: right sum is 28 minus 11 minus 6 equals 11. Left 11 equals right 11, so index 3 is the balance point. We return 3.

The balance point for Rajesh is index 3, where the left side 1, 7, 3 sums to 11 and the right side 5, 6 sums to 11.

2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Index 1: left=1 right=20
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Index 2: left=8 right=17
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Index 3: left=11 right=11

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: settlements [1,7,3,6,5,6]
    │
    ▼
  SettlementBalancer.findBalancePoint()
    │ pass 1: total = 28
    │ pass 2: leftSum=0
    │
    ├─ i=0 v=1  right=28-0-1=27   left0≠27  leftSum=1
    ├─ i=1 v=7  right=28-1-7=20   left1≠20  leftSum=8
    ├─ i=2 v=3  right=28-8-3=17   left8≠17  leftSum=11
    └─ i=3 v=6  right=28-11-6=11  left11==11 ✓ PIVOT
    │
    ▼
  Output: 3  (left [1,7,3]=11 == right [5,6]=11)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pivot index problem asks for the leftmost index where the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it, with the element at the index belonging to neither side, and I solve it in linear time with a single running prefix sum. I first compute the total of the array in one pass, then scan left to right keeping a running left sum of everything strictly before the current index. At each index the right sum is simply the total minus the left sum minus the current element, so I check whether the left sum equals that right sum and return the index immediately on the first match, giving me the leftmost pivot naturally.

The detail I always make explicit is that the current element is excluded from both sides, which is exactly why the right sum subtracts the current element once from the total. I also note the end cases: the first index is a pivot when everything after it is zero, since the empty left side counts as zero, and likewise for the last index. Negatives are fully supported because I am comparing sums rather than relying on any window monotonicity.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the settlement operations team. We laid out a day's sequence of net settlement amounts and found the earliest balance-point transaction where the total before it equaled the total after it, excluding that transaction, and we used that point to split the day's batch into two halves of equal net value for parallel downstream processing. Precomputing the total once and keeping a single running left sum found the split point in a single linear scan, which kept the batch-splitting step fast on large batches.

The senior-level point I make is that this is prefix sums in their simplest form, needing only one running total rather than a stored map, which is a nice contrast with the subarray-sum-equals-k problem that does need a map, and being able to explain when a map is and is not required shows I understand the technique rather than applying it blindly. I also mention accumulating the total and running sum in a long to avoid overflow on large monetary batches, and that returning on the first match is what gives the leftmost answer without extra bookkeeping. Drawing that distinction between the map and no-map prefix-sum variants is what signals real understanding to an interviewer.
